gajacchāyā
(‘shadow of an elephant’)
------------------------------------------
In the Hindu calendars, certain combinations of lunar days and asterisms are considered as very good. The गजच्छाया is one such. When the मोओन् is in the Maghā or Makhā नक्षत्र (the 10th constellation of 5 स्तर्स्) and the sun in the Hastā (the 13th constellation, also of 5 स्तर्स्), the period is considered as very sacred, especially for the performance of śrāddhas.
The śrāddha recommended here is to be performed in the shadow of an elephant. Hence the name (gaja = elephant; छाया = shadow). It is said to give gratification to the manes for thousands of kalpas (extraordinarily long periods of time).
This śrāddha can be performed during the intercalary months (adhika or मल māsa) also.

Gajāsura
(‘the demon [in the form of a] गज or elephant’)
------------------------------------------
He was the son of महिषासुर, the demon in the form of a bison, who was ultimately killed by the goddess दुर्गा.
Gajāsura pleased शिव with his auste-rities performed with devotion and secured several supernatural boons. Armed with the might of these, he started harassing the gods in हेअवेन्. When they supplicated to शिव himself for succour and protection, शिव challenged गजासुर for a duel. गजासुर surrendered with the condition that शिव should wear his skin as his apparel after killing him. शिव obliged him by doing so. Hence he came to be known by such names as Gajacarmāmbaradhara or Nāgacarmadhara or Kṛttivāsa (the wearer of the skin of गजासुर as his dress), Gajaghna (the killer of गजासुर) and so on.

gaja
(‘that which roars [due to the arrogance of strength]’, ‘an elephant’)
------------------------------------------
The गज or an elephant is a familiar figure met with in Hindu म्य्थोलोग्य् and other religious literature. Being the biggest and the most powerful of all the animals on land, it might have induced awe in the minds of the aboriginal people. According to one guess, this might have been the origin of the elephant-headed god गणपति and his cult.
Even by the time of the Aitareya Brāhmaṇa (8.22), use of tamed and trained elephants in warfare, was common.
Possessing elephants was often a symbol of one’s wealth and power. It was a must for a king or an emperor who would have an elephant (generally a white elephant) as the State elephant after a ritual baptism. This would then invariably be a part of his entourage on all important occasions.
The Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa (

.3-4) ascribes a divine origin to the elephant as being evolved out of मार्त्ताण्ड, a son of अदिति, the मोथेर् of gods.
Eight mythical elephants are supposed to be carrying this earth on their shoulders. They are: ऐरावत, Puṇḍarīka, वामन, Kumuda, Añjana, Puṣpadanta, Sārvabhauma and Supratīka.
Elephants formed one of the four divisions of an army (caturaṅgabala) of a king, the other three being horses, chariots and infantry.
The elephant is listed among the अष्टमङ्गलस्, eight objects signifying auspiciousness. (See AṢṬAMAṄGALAS.)
Elephants are often shown in the motifs on the walls of temples.

Gajalakṣmī
(‘Lakṣmī [associated with] elephants’)
------------------------------------------
Gajalakṣmī is the most popular of the eight forms of Lakṣmī—called Aṣṭamahālakṣmī—and is usually shown on the lintels of door-frames. She is dressed in snow-white garments and is seated on a lotus of eight petals. She has four arms carrying a long-stalked lotus, a pot of nectar, a बिल्व fruit (Aegle marmelos) and a conch. Behind her are two decorated elephants shown as pouring water over her from pots held in their trunks. The elephants may also be shown with raised trunks, holding a lotus each, in adoration.
One of the well-known figures is in the stone relief of the Varāhamaṇḍapa at Māmallāpuram (Mahābalipuram) near Chennai (or Madras).

Gajendra-mokṣa
(‘liberation of the king of elephants’)
------------------------------------------
One of the most famous episodes in the mythological literature of the Hindus is the story of the लिबेरतिओन् of Gajendra or the elephant king from the death grip of a crocodile.
Indradyumna, the king of the Pāṇḍyan country once ignored the great sage अगस्त्य and was cursed by him to be born as an elephant. Consequently he reincarnated as Gajendra, the king of the elephants in the region of the Trikūṭa-parvata (a mountain with three peaks). On a hot day in summer he went to a lake, along with all his tribe and was enjoying himself. At that time a crocodile caught his foot and started dragging him into water. All the heroic efforts of Gajendra and his herd to be freed from its clutches came to a nought and he started collapsing. At that time, he remembered the Lord विष्णु and prayed to him intensely. The Lord arrived there on his mount गरुड, discharged his famous discus-weapon, the सुदर्शन, thereby killing the crocodile and thus liberating the elephant king.
This episode (vide Bhāgavata 8.4 ) is now well-known as ‘Gajendra-मोक्ष’ and has supplied the core material for many a devotional composition, depicting ‘ārta-भक्ति’ or ‘devotion of the distressed’.
The prayer of Gajendra, spread over 31 verses (

-32) contains not only high philosophy of advaita but also extreme devotion. The ceremonial recitation of this section is common among the devotees of विष्णु.
The chief lesson of this section is that no disrespect should ever be shown to the devotees of the Lord.
See also INDRADYUMNA.

gajahasta
(‘hand-pose [resembling the] trunk of an elephant’)
------------------------------------------
In the मूर्तिशिल्पशास्त्र or इचोनोग्रफ्य्, one of the important aspects of the subject dealt with is the हस्त or the pose of the hand. Out of the several poses mentioned, the ‘gajahasta’ is also one. It is called so because of its resemblance to the trunk of an elephant (gaja = elephant, हस्त = hand or trunk).
Gajahasta in images is shown in two different ways. In the first, the arm is shown dangling by the side. Usually the left arm of the images of देवी is shown in this way. In the second the arm may be shown across the chest, with the hand bent down, as is seen in the images of नटराज (the left normal arm).
